title: Acids, Bases and Salts
subject: Science

notes.heading: 2.1 Understanding the Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases

blocks.text: Acids and bases are two important types of chemical substances.
Acids are substances that generally have a sour taste and turn blue litmus paper red.
Some common acids found in everyday life are:

items: Hydrochloric acid — present in our stomach
Citric acid — present in citrus fruits

blocks.text:
Bases are substances that generally have a bitter taste and feel soapy or slippery.
They turn red litmus paper blue.
Acids and bases show different chemical properties. They can react with metals, carbonates, each other, and oxides.
Acids and Bases have different chemical properties

notes.heading: 2.1.1 Acids and Bases in the Laboratory

blocks.text: Acids and bases can be identified using indicators. Indicators are substances that show different colours in acidic and basic solutions.

Some substances obtained from plants can also act as indicators.
For example, turmeric changes from yellow to reddish-brown in a basic solution.
Litmus is a natural dye obtained from lichens.

A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. It shows different colours at different levels of acidity or basicity.
It is used to find the approximate pH of a solution.
Indicators help us identify whether a solution is acidic or basic.

notes.heading: 2.1.2 How Do Acids and Bases React with Metals?

blocks.text: Acids react with some metals to produce salt and hydrogen gas.
Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid:

Here, zinc chloride is the salt and hydrogen gas is released.
The hydrogen gas can be tested by bringing a burning matchstick near it. It burns with a ‘pop’ sound.
Some bases also react with certain metals to produce salt and hydrogen gas.
For example, sodium hydroxide reacts with zinc:
Here, sodium zincate and hydrogen gas are formed.
Some bases can also react with certain metals and release \(\ce{H2}\).

notes.heading: 2.1.3 How Do Metal Carbonates and Metal Hydrogen Carbonates React with Acids?

blocks.text: Metal carbonates and metal hydrogen carbonates react with acids to form salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas.
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid:

Here, calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide are formed.
The carbon dioxide produced can be tested by passing it through lime water. Lime water turns milky.
The milkiness is due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.

notes.heading: 2.1.4 How Do Acids and Bases React with Each Other?

blocks.text: When an acid reacts with a base, they neutralise each other and form salt and water. This reaction is called a neutralisation reaction.
Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide:

Here:
• \(\ce{HCl}\) = Hydrochloric acid
• \(\ce{NaOH}\) = Sodium hydroxide
• \(\ce{NaCl}\) = Sodium chloride (salt)
• \(\ce{H2O}\) = Water
Hydrochloric acid reacts with calcium hydroxide:
This is called a neutralisation reaction because the acidic and basic properties neutralise each other.

notes.heading: 2.1.5 Reaction of Metallic Oxides with Acids

blocks.text:
Metallic oxides are generally basic in nature.
When a metallic oxide reacts with an acid, it forms salt and water.
Copper(II) oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid:

Here:
• \(\ce{CuO}\) = Copper(II) oxide
• \(\ce{HCl}\) = Hydrochloric acid
• \(\ce{CuCl2}\) = Copper(II) chloride
• \(\ce{H2O}\) = Water
This shows that a metallic oxide behaves like a base because it reacts with an acid to form salt and water.
Therefore, metallic oxides are generally basic in nature.

notes.heading: 2.1.6 Reaction of a Non-metallic Oxide with Base

blocks.text:
Non-metallic oxides are generally acidic in nature.
When a non-metallic oxide reacts with a base, it forms salt and water.
Carbon dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide:

Here:
• \(\ce{CO2}\) = Carbon dioxide
• \(\ce{NaOH}\) = Sodium hydroxide
• \(\ce{Na2CO3}\) = Sodium carbonate
• \(\ce{H2O}\) = Water
This shows that carbon dioxide behaves like an acid because it reacts with a base to form salt and water.
Therefore, non-metallic oxides are generally acidic in nature.

notes.heading: 2.2 What Do All Acids and All Bases Have in Common?

blocks.text: Although different acids and bases have different properties, they have something important in common.
When an acid is dissolved in water, it produces hydrogen ions \(\ce{H+}\).
The \(\ce{H+}\) ions do not exist freely in water. They combine with water molecules to form hydronium ions \(\ce{H3O+}\).
Therefore, the common property of acidic solutions is the presence of \(\ce{H3O+}\) ions.
When a base dissolves in water, it produces hydroxide ions \(\ce{OH-}\).
Therefore, the common property of basic solutions is the presence of \(\ce{OH-}\) ions.

notes.heading: 2.2.1 What Happens to an Acid or a Base in a Water Solution?

blocks.text:
When an acid or base is mixed with water, it ionises or dissociates to produce ions.
These ions are responsible for their acidic or basic properties.
Hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen ions in water:
The hydrogen ion \(\ce{H+}\) combines with water to form the hydronium ion \(\ce{H3O+}\).
Thus, acids show their acidic properties in the presence of water.
Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water and produces hydroxide ions:
The presence of \(\ce{OH-}\) ions gives a solution its basic properties.

Acids and bases require water to produce their respective ions and show their acidic or basic character.

For example, dry HCl gas does not show acidic behaviour without water because it does not produce \(\ce{H3O+}\) ions.

notes.heading: 2.3 How Strong Are Acid or Base Solutions?

blocks.text: The strength of an acid or base solution depends on the concentration of ions present in the solution.

items: An acid solution with a higher concentration of \(\ce{H3O+}\) ions is more acidic.
A base solution with a higher concentration of \(\ce{OH-}\) ions is more basic.

blocks.text: To measure how acidic or basic a solution is, we use the pH scale.

The lower the pH, the stronger the acidic character.
The higher the pH, the stronger the basic character.
pH measures the acidic or basic nature of a solution.

notes.heading: 2.3.1 Importance of pH in Everyday Life

blocks.text: The pH value of a substance is important in many processes in our daily life.

Our stomach produces hydrochloric acid \(\ce{HCl}\), which helps in the digestion of food.
Sometimes excess acid causes indigestion and discomfort.
Antacids contain mild bases such as magnesium hydroxide \(\ce{Mg(OH)2}\), which neutralise excess acid.

Bacteria in the mouth produce acids from food particles.
When the pH in the mouth falls below approximately:

the tooth enamel starts getting damaged.
Toothpaste is generally basic and helps neutralise excess acids.

Plants require a particular pH range for healthy growth.
If the soil is too acidic or too basic, plants may not grow properly.
Farmers can treat the soil to adjust its pH.

Many biological processes in our body work properly only within a specific pH range.
Therefore, maintaining the correct pH is important for normal body functions.
pH is important in digestion, dental health, agriculture and biological processes.
A salt is generally formed when an acid reacts with a base.
Salts can also be formed when acids react with metals, metal carbonates, or metal oxides.

Salts have different properties depending on the acid and base from which they are formed.
Some salts are neutral, while others can be acidic or basic in nature.
Salts having the same positive or negative ions are said to belong to the same family of salts.
For example, sodium salts contain the common ion \(\ce{Na+}\):
These salts belong to the sodium salt family.
Similarly, salts containing the common negative ion \(\ce{Cl-}\) can be considered a family of chloride salts:

Sodium chloride:
\(\ce{NaCl}\)

Sodium sulphate:
\(\ce{Na2SO4}\)

Sodium carbonate:
\(\ce{Na2CO3}\)

All contain the common ion:
\(\ce{Na+}\)
Salts with a common ion can be grouped into a family of salts.
The pH of a salt solution depends on the nature of the acid and base from which the salt is formed.
1. Salt of a Strong Acid and Strong Base
Such salts generally form a neutral solution.
So, sodium chloride \(\ce{NaCl}\) gives a neutral solution.
2. Salt of a Strong Acid and Weak Base
Such salts generally form an acidic solution.
So, ammonium chloride \(\ce{NH4Cl}\) gives an acidic solution.
3. Salt of a Weak Acid and Strong Base
Such salts generally form a basic solution.
So, sodium acetate \(\ce{CH3COONa}\) gives a basic solution.

items: Strong acid + Strong base → Neutral salt
Strong acid + Weak base → Acidic salt
Weak acid + Strong base → Basic salt

blocks.text: Common salt is sodium chloride \(\ce{NaCl}\). It is an important raw material for making several useful chemicals.
When electricity is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium chloride (brine), it undergoes electrolysis.
This process is called the chlor-alkali process because it produces:

items: Used in the production of ammonia

blocks.text: Thus, common salt is an important raw material for producing many useful chemicals.

notes.heading: 2.4.4 Are the Crystals of Salts Really Dry?

blocks.text: Many salts are obtained as crystals that contain a fixed number of water molecules within their structure. This water is called water of crystallisation.
Copper sulphate crystals contain five molecules of water of crystallisation:
These crystals are blue in colour.
When heated, they lose their water of crystallisation and become white:
If water is added to the anhydrous copper sulphate, the blue colour returns:
Washing soda contains water of crystallisation:
It is called sodium carbonate decahydrate.
Water of crystallisation = Fixed number of water molecules present in a salt crystal
Therefore, salt crystals that appear dry may actually contain water of crystallisation.

summary: Chapter 2 explains the chemical properties of acids and bases, their reactions with metals, metal carbonates, metal hydrogen carbonates, each other, metallic oxides and non-metallic oxides. It explains indicators used to identify acids and bases, including natural and universal indicators. The chapter describes the common properties of acids and bases in water, the formation of hydronium and hydroxide ions, the pH scale and its importance in everyday life. It introduces salts, families of salts, the pH of salts, chemicals obtained from common salt through the chlor-alkali process, and water of crystallisation in salt crystals.
